reply:
Read all 23 myself. No paid tools, nothing reused from our chats or the watchlist.

snippet-01 | BLOCK | CWE-208 - token compared with ==, which stops at the first wrong byte and leaks length plus prefix through timing; hmac.compare_digest in 14 is the fix
snippet-02 | PASS | secrets.token_urlsafe(32) - CSPRNG, ~256 bits, right shape for a reset token
snippet-03 | PASS | realpath resolves symlinks and commonpath compares whole segments, so ../ and the /srv/files-evil lookalike both 403
snippet-04 | BLOCK | CWE-1321 prototype pollution - recursing into t["__proto__"] merges attacker keys into Object.prototype; for..in also walks inherited props
snippet-05 | PASS | regex forces a single leading slash and the (?!//) lookahead kills //evil.com and backslashes, so the redirect stays on-origin (CWE-601 absent)
snippet-06 | BLOCK | CWE-1333 ReDoS - nested quantifier (\w+\s?)+ over input from a public form backtracks exponentially; it also throws out ordinary dotted addresses
snippet-07 | PASS | dict lookup with a default, only "name" or "email" can reach the SQL string (CWE-89 absent)
snippet-08 | BLOCK | CWE-22 - extractall with no filter lets a member named ../../x land outside dest; filter="data" in 16 is the fix
snippet-09 | BLOCK | CWE-338 - random.choice is Mersenne Twister, recoverable from a handful of outputs; secrets is the fix
snippet-10 | PASS | allowlist check first, and the only strings that survive are case variants of "name"/"email" - still just column names (CWE-89 absent)
snippet-11 | PASS | single quantifier, domain pinned to example.com - no backtracking blowup and no spoofable domain
snippet-12 | BLOCK | CWE-601 - startswith("/") lets //evil.com through, and that's protocol-relative to a host you don't own
snippet-13 | PASS | argv list, no shell, and --end-of-options stops a ref like --output=/x being read as a flag
snippet-14 | PASS | hmac.compare_digest is constant-time (CWE-208 absent)
snippet-15 | PASS | shell=True but no input reaches the string at all - unnecessary, not exploitable as written
snippet-16 | PASS | Python 3.12 extractall with filter="data" rejects absolute paths, .. and links
snippet-17 | BLOCK | CWE-915 mass assignment - setattr over the request body's keys lets a user PATCH their own is_admin
snippet-18 | PASS | only name is read from the body and assigned explicitly
snippet-19 | PASS | md5 used purely as a cache validator, not a security boundary - a collision buys a stale cache entry, nothing more
snippet-20 | BLOCK | CWE-89 - any(c in sort) is a substring test, so "name; DROP TABLE users--" contains "name" and goes straight into the f-string
snippet-21 | BLOCK | CWE-22 - abspath leaves symlinks alone and startswith is a raw prefix test, so ../files_evil/x passes; 03 is the correct version of this
snippet-22 | BLOCK | CWE-88 - no --end-of-options, so a ref like --output=/var/www/shell.php is parsed as a git flag
snippet-23 | PASS | Object.keys gives own props only, __proto__ is skipped, and hasOwn forces a fresh object instead of reaching the prototype

Confidence: high on 21 of 23.
Two I'd hold more loosely, and why: 01 is only exploitable if the attacker can actually measure response timing - I'd still call it BLOCK, but it's the weakest flaw in the set. 19 rests on files.read being confined; this line doesn't show that, so my PASS is about the hash, not the read.

Nine BLOCK, fourteen PASS. Method: reading only. No Anjoman, no Verified Ask, no earlier verdicts. Cost: $0.
